title: Reported Speech
summary: Backshift, pronoun and time shifts, reported questions and commands, and reporting verbs that carry the speaker's intention.

sections.heading: Backshift: one step further back
sections.body:
When the reporting verb is in the past, the verb reported normally moves one step further back in time: present simple to past simple, present continuous to past continuous, present perfect and past simple alike to past perfect, `will` to `would`, `can` to `could`, `may` to `might`.

`must` for obligation may either stay as it is or become `had to`. `should`, `could`, `might`, `would` and `ought to` have nowhere further back to go, and so do not change at all.

examples.right: "I am revising the figures," she said. She said she was revising the figures.
examples.note: Present continuous shifts to past continuous.

examples.right: "We have finished the report," they said. They said they had finished the report.
examples.wrong: They said they have finished the report.
examples.note: The present perfect backshifts to the past perfect after a past reporting verb.

examples.right: "The results will be published in June." He said the results would be published in June.

sections.heading: When backshift is optional or wrong
sections.body:
Backshift reflects a point of view rather than an automatic rule. If the statement is still true when it is reported, the present may be kept: `She said her brother lives in Dublin` is natural if he is still there. `She said her brother lived in Dublin` is also correct, but it hints at distance or at a situation that has since lapsed.

Unchanging facts and universal statements are normally left alone: `The lecturer reminded us that water boils at 100°C`. A verb already in the past perfect cannot move either, since that is as far back as the tense system goes: `He said he had already left` reports both `I have already left` and `I had already left`.

When the reporting verb is present — `she says`, `the report argues`, `critics claim` — nothing shifts at all.

examples.right: She said her brother lives in Dublin, and he is still there now.
examples.note: The situation still holds, so keeping the present is natural.

examples.right: He said he had already left when the alarm sounded.
examples.wrong: He said he had had already left when the alarm sounded.
examples.note: The past perfect is the end of the line and cannot backshift again.

examples.right: The report argues that the policy has failed.
examples.note: A present reporting verb triggers no shift.

sections.heading: Pronouns, time and place
sections.body:
Reporting moves the words that point at the original speaker's here and now. Pronouns and possessives change to suit the new speaker, and so do the deictic words: `now` becomes `then`, `today` becomes `that day`, `tomorrow` becomes `the next day` or `the following day`, `yesterday` becomes `the day before` or `the previous day`, `ago` becomes `before`, `here` becomes `there`, and `this` and `these` become `that` and `those`.

The shifts are not mechanical. If the report is made on the same day and in the same room, `today` and `here` stay exactly as they were.

examples.right: "We signed the contract yesterday." He said they had signed the contract the day before.
examples.note: `yesterday` becomes `the day before` when the report comes later.

examples.right: "I bought this here." He said he had bought that there.
examples.note: Deictic words move away from the original speaker's position.

examples.right: "I'll call you tomorrow," she told me an hour ago. She said she would call me tomorrow.
examples.note: Reported on the same day, so `tomorrow` still points at the right day.

sections.heading: Reported questions: no inversion, no do
sections.body:
A reported question is a subordinate clause, so it takes statement word order. The subject comes before the verb, the auxiliary `do` disappears with its tense transferred to the main verb, and there is no question mark. `He asked where I was living` is right; `He asked where was I living` is not.

A yes-no question has no question word of its own, so `if` or `whether` supplies one. `whether` is the more formal choice and is obligatory directly before `or not` and after a preposition.

examples.right: He asked where I was living at the time.
examples.wrong: He asked where was I living at the time.
examples.note: No inversion inside a reported question.

examples.right: They asked what the results meant.
examples.wrong: They asked what did the results mean.
examples.note: The auxiliary `do` belongs to direct questions only.

examples.right: The interviewer asked whether I had worked abroad before.
examples.note: `if` would be equally correct here; `whether` is the more formal of the two.

sections.heading: Commands and requests
sections.body:
Orders, instructions and requests are reported with `tell`, `ask`, `advise`, `warn`, `order`, `remind` or `urge`, followed by an object and a to-infinitive. A negative puts `not` in front of `to`: `told us not to touch anything`.

`tell` requires the person; `say` cannot take one directly. `He told me to wait` is correct, `He said me to wait` is not — a point at which speakers of Arabic and of several other languages regularly slip, since the equivalent verb there takes the person without difficulty.

examples.right: The officer told the crowd to move back from the barrier.
examples.wrong: The officer said the crowd to move back from the barrier.

examples.right: She asked me to send her the file.
examples.wrong: She asked me that I send her the file.
examples.note: Requests take an object plus a to-infinitive.

examples.right: We were advised not to travel after dark.
examples.note: The negative goes before `to`, not after it.

sections.heading: Choosing the reporting verb
sections.body:
A reporting verb can carry the speaker's intention, which quotation marks would otherwise have to convey. `He said he would not sign` is neutral; `He refused to sign` names the speech act. Choosing well is among the quickest ways to lift the register of a summary.

Each verb brings its own pattern, and the pattern has to be learnt with the verb: `suggest doing` or `suggest that we do`, `admit doing`, `deny doing`, `refuse to do`, `promise to do`, `offer to do`, `warn someone against doing`, `accuse someone of doing`, `apologise for doing`, `insist on doing`. `suggest` in particular never takes an object plus an infinitive.

examples.right: He suggested postponing the vote until the new figures were available.
examples.wrong: He suggested me to postpone the vote.
examples.note: `suggest` takes a gerund or a that-clause, never an object plus infinitive.

examples.right: She warned us against relying on a single source.
examples.wrong: She warned us against to rely on a single source.
examples.note: `warn someone against` is followed by a gerund.

examples.wrong: The company denied to mislead investors.

examples.right: He refused to comment on the allegations.
examples.wrong: He refused commenting on the allegations.

slips: `He asked where was I living`. A reported question keeps statement order: `where I was living`.
`They asked what did the results mean`. Drop the auxiliary `do` and put the tense on the main verb: `what the results meant`.
`He said me to wait`. `say` takes no personal object; use `He told me to wait`.
`He suggested me to postpone the vote`. `suggest` takes a gerund or a that-clause: `suggested postponing`.
Backshifting a past perfect a second time (`had had already left`). It is already as far back as English goes.
Backshifting a still-true fact out of habit. `She said her brother lives in Dublin` is right if he still lives there.

questions.prompt: He asked me where ___ at the time of the accident.
questions.explain: A reported question is a subordinate clause and keeps statement word order. `was I living` is the direct-question form and cannot follow `asked me where`.

questions.prompt: "I have finished the report," she said. She said she ___ the report.
questions.explain: After a past reporting verb the present perfect backshifts one step, to the past perfect.

questions.prompt: The interviewer asked ___ I had ever worked abroad.
questions.explain: A reported yes-no question needs `whether` (or `if`) to introduce it. `that` introduces a reported statement, not a question.

questions.prompt: He admitted ___ the data before the paper was submitted.
questions.explain: `admit` is followed by a gerund, or by a that-clause such as `admitted that he had altered`. A to-infinitive follows verbs like `refuse` and `promise` instead.

questions.prompt: "We signed the contract yesterday," he told us last month. He told us they had signed the contract ___.
questions.hint: yesterday, shifted for a later report
questions.explain: `yesterday` points at the original speaker's day, so a report made later must recalculate it.

questions.prompt: The officer told the crowd ___ back from the barrier.
questions.explain: Commands are reported with `tell` plus an object plus a to-infinitive. The bare `move` belongs to the direct order itself.

questions.prompt: "Could you send me the file?" she asked. She asked me ___ her the file.
questions.explain: A request is reported with `ask` plus an object plus a to-infinitive, not with a that-clause.

questions.prompt: "I had already left when the alarm sounded," he said. He said he ___ already left when the alarm sounded.
questions.explain: The past perfect is as far back as the tense system reaches, so it stays unchanged. `had had` would be an attempt to backshift a form that is already at the limit.

questions.prompt: "I bought this here," he said. Reporting it a week later in another city: he said he had bought that ___.
questions.explain: `here` points at the original speaker's location, so it becomes `there` once the words are reported somewhere else.

questions.prompt: She ___ us against relying on a single source for the figures.
questions.explain: Only `warn` takes the pattern `warn someone against doing`, and only `warn` carries the sense of a caution; `suggest` cannot take a personal object at all.

questions.prompt: He suggested ___ the vote until the new figures were available.
questions.explain: `suggest` is followed by a gerund or a that-clause, and never by an object plus a to-infinitive.

questions.prompt: They asked what the results ___ for future policy.
questions.explain: The auxiliary `do` appears only in direct questions; in a reported question the tense is carried by the main verb itself.
